_comment: Illustrative worked examples for the annotation codebook. These are NOT benchmark queries and never enter the benchmark. build_annotation_materials.js verifies that every cited corpus id exists in the win32-visible corpus, that OOD examples' absent_terms appear in no corpus record, and that no example is identical or near-identical to any v0.1/v0.2 benchmark query.

examples.query: make a zip of this folder
examples.label: CLEAR

readings.reading: create a zip archive of a folder

examples.why: One reading, one record that performs it. Nothing else in the list zips a folder.

examples.label: CLEAR
examples.why: The request names both the tool and the task. The other pip records (install, list, uninstall) do different things and essentially nobody who writes these words wants them.

examples.query: which process is eating my CPU
examples.label: CLEAR

readings.reading: see which processes use the most CPU

examples.why: Two records, but both sort processes by CPU: same effect, different wording. Equivalent records are variants of one task, not ambiguity. (tac-0219 'show cpu info' answers a different question and is not a plausible reading of these words.)

examples.label: CLEAR
examples.why: Two supported readings exist, but the words name a compose stack. Almost nobody who writes this wants every running container stopped, so the second reading fails the plausibility test (Step 3). One dominant reading: CLEAR.

examples.label: AMBIGUOUS
examples.why: A bare tool name: it names no task. Four records for it perform four different tasks, so no reading can be dominant. AMBIGUOUS by the bare-name rule (Section 6.1).

examples.label: AMBIGUOUS

readings.reading: follow the logs of all docker compose services

examples.why: Containers run under different tools (docker, docker compose, Kubernetes), each with its own record, and a user of one is badly served by another: a different scope or ecosystem makes a distinct task. The word container rules out readings such as a log file on this machine, so those are not counted.

examples.label: AMBIGUOUS
examples.why: Three cleanups, each a common reading of "free up space", and each destroys something different (images can be re-pulled; volumes hold data). Readings that differ in effect on your data are distinct tasks (Section 6.3), and a user who meant one is badly served by another.

examples.query: download this installer from the website
examples.label: CLEAR

readings.reading: download a file from a web address
resume a download that was interrupted

examples.why: A plain download is the dominant reading; tac-0010 and tac-0107 both save a web address to a file, so they are variants. Resuming an interrupted download is a narrower task that few users mean by these words, so it fails the plausibility test.

examples.label: OOD
examples.why: A real terminal task, but no record compiles a Rust project or any other program. OOD means "the list cannot perform this", not "a shell cannot".

examples.query: reserve a table at an Italian restaurant
examples.label: OOD
examples.why: Not a computing task at all.

examples.query: set up nginx as a reverse proxy
examples.label: OOD
examples.why: The tool is absent from the list. Do not label it by what a shell could do.

examples.query: rename every file in this folder to lowercase
examples.label: OOD
examples.why: Borderline. tac-0141 renames ONE file. Filling in placeholders is allowed, but turning it into a loop over every file changes the command's structure, so the record does not perform this task.

examples.query: encrypt a file with a password
examples.label: CLEAR

readings.reading: encrypt a file symmetrically with gpg

examples.why: The list can do this (tac-0364 asks for a passphrase). A task that is done differently in real life is still CLEAR if a record performs it.
